q: In Lean, who defines value?
why: Lean starts by defining value from the customer's point of view.

q: A maker-checker approval required by regulation is best classified as…
why: It is required but not directly valued by the customer: minimize it, don't remove it.

q: Re-keying the same data into two systems is…
why: Duplicate data entry adds no value and introduces errors.

q: Which is one of Lean's five principles?
why: Value, value stream, flow, pull and perfection.

q: What does the 'W' in TIMWOODS stand for?
why: Transportation, Inventory, Motion, Waiting, Overproduction, Over-processing, Defects, Skills.

q: A daily report that nobody reads is which waste?
why: Producing output that isn't needed is overproduction.

q: A queue of 1,200 breaks waiting for review is which waste?
why: Unprocessed work piling up is inventory.

q: Three people check the same low-risk item when one check is enough. Which waste?
why: Doing more work than required is over-processing.

q: Skilled analysts spend half their day copying data between spreadsheets. Which waste is most obvious?
why: Not using people's abilities is the 8th waste, often alongside motion and transportation.

q: What does DMAIC stand for?
why: DMAIC is the Six Sigma improvement cycle.

q: In which DMAIC phase do you establish the baseline performance?
why: Measure captures current performance before changes.

q: SOPs, control charts and training to sustain gains belong to which phase?
why: Control makes sure the improvement sticks.

q: What defect rate does 'six sigma' quality correspond to?
why: Six sigma is about 3.4 DPMO.

q: Six Sigma primarily focuses on reducing…
why: Lean targets waste and speed; Six Sigma targets variation and defects.

q: Which approach is used to design a brand-new process rather than improve an existing one?
why: DMADV: Define, Measure, Analyze, Design, Verify.

q: What does FMEA help you do?
options: Prioritize how a process could fail by severity, occurrence and detection
why: FMEA scores failure modes to focus prevention efforts.

q: What are the four steps of the Deming cycle?
why: PDCA is a simple loop for continuous improvement.

q: What does 'kaizen' mean?
why: Kaizen is continuous, incremental improvement by everyone.

q: A dropdown list that prevents users entering an invalid currency code is an example of…
why: Poka-yoke designs processes so errors can't happen.

q: 'Go to gemba' means…
options: Go and see the work where it actually happens
why: Gemba is the real place where value is created.

q: In 5S, what comes after Sort and Set in order?
why: Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardize, Sustain.

q: 300 breaks are open and the team closes 100 per day. What is the average lead time by Little's Law?
why: Lead time = WIP ÷ throughput = 300 ÷ 100 = 3 days.

q: Turnaround falls from 5 days to 4 days. What is the percentage reduction?
Takt time is…
why: Takt time is the pace needed to meet demand.

q: According to Little's Law, how can you cut lead time without adding staff?
why: Lower WIP with the same throughput means shorter lead time.

q: Why does standardization come before improvement?
options: You can't reliably improve a process that everyone does differently
It removes the need for training
why: Standard work reduces variation and gives a baseline to improve from.

q: Which item belongs in a good SOP?
options: Exception handling steps and escalation paths
why: SOPs must cover decision points, exceptions, controls and escalation.

q: What is the best way to test a new SOP?
options: Ask someone new to follow it and see where they get stuck
Have the author read it again
why: A newcomer reveals unclear or missing steps.

q: Which writing style suits an SOP?
options: Plain, active instructions: 'Open the Unmatched Items screen'
why: Clear, active steps are easy to follow.

q: Which process is the best candidate for RPA?
options: High-volume, rule-based, stable, with structured digital data
A process that changes every week
Handwritten paper forms with unique layouts
why: RPA suits repetitive, rule-based, stable work.

q: Why should you simplify a process before automating it?
options: Automating a broken process just produces errors faster
why: Fix and standardize first, then automate.

q: Before switching on a new matching rule, what should you do?
options: Test it on historical data to check for false matches
Turn it on in production immediately
Ask users to guess its accuracy
why: A false automatic match is worse than no match; test first.

q: A matching rule that accepts amount differences under $1 for bank fees is a…
why: Tolerance rules allow small, approved differences.

q: Why measure a baseline before making a change?
options: Without it you can't prove the improvement
why: Improvement is measured against the baseline.

q: Breaks fell sharply in the week after a change, but volumes also dropped for a holiday. What should you do?
options: Account for the volume change and measure over a longer period
why: Control for other factors and look for a sustained trend.

q: An interviewer asks about an improvement you quoted. What should you be ready to explain?
options: The baseline, measurement method, period and your specific actions
why: Interviewers probe numbers to check they're real and that you understand them.
